models.section: 2 Mapping Crime and the Road Metric
models.family: network shortest-path metric with local connectors
models.purpose: Approximate automobile travel cost between arbitrary map points while allowing either a highway-assisted route or a side-street-only route.
models.summary: The paper maps highway entrances and exits to graph vertices, road sections to Euclidean-length edges, uses Manhattan connectors between grid points and graph vertices, and takes the minimum of the best highway-assisted route and a direct Manhattan route.

variables.definition: First arbitrary point on the map.
Second arbitrary point on the map.
Candidate highway entrance or exit used to enter the graph route.
Candidate highway entrance or exit used to leave the graph route.
Manhattan distance used for side-street travel and the direct non-highway alternative.
Dijkstra shortest-path length between two highway vertices using Euclidean edge weights.
Minimum road cost between two map points.
Number of rows in the map grid.
Number of columns in the map grid.

governing_equations.purpose: Choose the lower-cost highway-assisted or direct side-street route.

equation_status.reason: The complete road-metric minimum is displayed on page 5 and visually checked at full resolution.

objectives: Minimize the route cost between each pair of grid points over highway-entry and highway-exit choices and the direct Manhattan alternative.
constraints: Highway sections use nonnegative Euclidean edge weights.
The route may avoid the highway entirely.

details: The metric is static and has no initial state.
Map extent and boundary handling are not reported.

parameter_estimation.method: No speeds, connector multipliers, turn costs, or calibration observations are fitted; edge costs are assigned from map geometry.
parameters: relative freeway versus side-street cost scaling

steps: Encode highway entrances/exits as vertices and intervening sections as weighted edges.
Compute Manhattan connector distances from grid points to vertices.
Run Dijkstra shortest paths between graph vertices.
Take the minimum route cost and store all grid-pair distances.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Not applicable to deterministic shortest paths; grid-resolution convergence is not tested.

assumptions: The offender travels primarily by automobile.
Drivers select shortest routes and use highways when beneficial.
Side-street time is proportional to Manhattan distance.
Freeway time is proportional to Euclidean section length.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The paper gives neither route-time observations nor relative mode-cost coefficients, so the travel-time interpretation is not identified; computational feasibility is asserted through grid precomputation without runtime or memory measurements.

validation_refs: Paper card verification and observation O-B-2010-7273-005
models.computational_cost: Dijkstra is invoked repeatedly and all grid-pair distances are stored; the paper calls this slow but gives no complexity, grid size, runtime, or memory measurement.
strengths: Creates one shared distance object for both target branches.
limitations: Uses geometric length as a travel-time proxy.
Omits direction, speed, congestion, turns, local-road topology, and multimodal travel.
No discretization or route-calibration evidence is supplied.
missing_details: m and n values and cell size

models.purpose: Construct a normalized spatial field for possible future crime locations from prior event locations and ages.
models.summary: The paper begins with a Euclidean Gaussian KDE, interprets its quadratic form as a metric, substitutes road distance into an exponential kernel, normalizes each event kernel, lets bandwidth increase with event age, and averages the kernels.

variables.definition: Map location at which the density is evaluated.
Location of incident i.
Time at which the density field is evaluated.
Occurrence time of incident i.
Number of incidents included at time t.
Matrix called a covariance matrix in the Euclidean baseline.
Baseline Gaussian kernel associated with A.
Road distance supplied by MU-B-7273-ROAD-METRIC.
Increasing bandwidth function of incident age.
Road-distance exponential kernel for one incident.
Integral used to normalize the ith road kernel.

variables.unit: inverse map-area or grid probability mass
variables.definition: Average time-dependent road-kernel field.

governing_equations.purpose: State the Euclidean KDE baseline.
Define the displayed two-dimensional Gaussian-style baseline kernel.
State the quadratic-form norm used by the paper to motivate metric substitution.
Define the road-distance kernel for incident i.
Normalize each road kernel over the map domain.
Specify the empirical increasing bandwidth function, with t measured in weeks.
Aggregate normalized incident kernels into the time-dependent density field.

equation_status.reason: Seven central baseline, adaptation, normalization, bandwidth, and aggregation equations are displayed on pages 5-6 and visually checked.

objectives: Estimate a spatial field that emphasizes recent incidents while allowing older kernels to diffuse.
constraints: Each incident kernel is divided by M_i(t).
Only incidents available by evaluation time should enter the sum.
h is increasing in incident age under the paper's chosen form.

details: An incident kernel begins sharply concentrated near its event location.
The integration domain and map-edge treatment are not specified.
The kernel field is not an equilibrium dynamical system.

parameter_estimation.method: The paper says h(t)=2.5 arctan(2t+0.2) was empirically a good fit but gives no loss, training cases, or sensitivity grid.

steps: Use precomputed road distances on the m by n grid.
Evaluate one normalized kernel per eligible incident.
Average the kernels for every grid cell and evaluation time.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: No grid-resolution, boundary-mass, or bandwidth convergence criterion is reported.

assumptions: Recent incidents are more informative than earlier incidents.
Kernel diffusion with age captures declining spatial relevance.
The road metric is suitable inside the kernel.
Selected incidents belong to one offender and approximate crime locations.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The three bandwidth constants are selected without a disclosed scoring protocol, and the road-cost scale is not tied to h units; normalization is formal but boundary and grid effects are untested.

models.computational_cost: Each included incident contributes a kernel at every grid cell; cost scales with incident count and grid size after road distances are precomputed, but no runtime is reported.
strengths: Provides a shared spatial representation for time and network accessibility.
Makes recency enter through a visible bandwidth function.
limitations: Bandwidth choice is not calibrated under a disclosed loss.
Boundary and grid normalization are unspecified.
The covariance-to-metric derivation contains a matrix-role inconsistency.
missing_details: Grid cell area and discrete normalizer
Unit mapping between d and h

models.purpose: Predict a future spatial field when one stationary density is judged inadequate for the whole crime series.
models.summary: For each grid cell, the paper constructs density snapshots just before successive incidents plus one intermediate post-history time, then fits a time-weighted linear regression and evaluates it at the future event time.

variables.definition: Fixed map cell for a pointwise temporal regression.
Location of incident i.
Occurrence time of incident i with increasing order.
Time of the last observed incident.
Future time at which the field is requested.
Chosen time between t_n and t^* used to add a diffused field.
Small offset used to evaluate fields just before later incidents.
Density value supplied by MU-B-7273-TEMPORAL-ROAD-KDE.
Pointwise linear-regression design matrix.
Matrix weighting later density snapshots more heavily.

variables.unit: density intercept and density per week
variables.definition: Estimated pointwise linear trend coefficients.
Vector of historical phi values at one grid cell.

governing_equations.purpose: Define chronological observations and a future evaluation time.
Specify pre-incident density snapshots used by the temporal fit.
Add a diffused field at an intermediate post-history time.
State the standard normal equations used as the baseline.

governing_equations.source_expression: X^t W X beta_hat = X^t W y
governing_equations.purpose: Estimate each grid cell's time-weighted linear density trend.

equation_status.reason: The chronological field sequence and both standard and weighted normal equations are displayed on pages 6-7.

objectives: Extrapolate a time-varying density field while giving later density snapshots greater influence.
constraints: Only incidents before an evaluation time enter each historical phi field.
A separate linear fit is performed at each grid cell.

details: Historical density fields are generated from the first available incidents.
No nonnegativity, mass-normalization, or map-boundary condition is imposed on the extrapolated field.
The model extrapolates a finite time trend rather than an equilibrium.

parameter_estimation.method: Weighted least squares is stated, with later fields weighted linearly in time; the exact W entries, epsilon, t_M selection, and design matrix are not printed.

steps: Construct historical phi fields using only incidents before each time.
Evaluate fields at t_2-epsilon through t_n-epsilon and at t_M.
At every grid cell, fit a weighted linear trend.
Evaluate the fitted trend at t^*.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: No conditioning, residual, rank, extrapolation-range, nonnegativity, or renormalization criterion is reported.

assumptions: Pointwise field values evolve approximately linearly over the fitted interval.
Later density snapshots deserve linearly greater weight.
A chosen future time t^* is available.
Independent cellwise fits are adequate despite spatial dependence.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The design and weights are incompletely specified, and the extrapolated vector is not constrained to remain a density; the paper provides no residual or conditioning evidence.

models.computational_cost: One weighted linear regression is performed per grid cell after repeated density-field evaluations; the paper gives no runtime or conditioning profile.
strengths: Makes temporal evolution explicit rather than assuming one static field.
States a past-only inclusion rule for historical fields.
Uses recency weights transparently in the normal equations.
limitations: Pointwise linear extrapolation ignores spatial covariance.
No nonnegativity or total-mass constraint preserves probability semantics.
The exact future event time is used in retrospective tests.
W, epsilon, and t_M are not reproducibly specified.

models.family: metric-space Fréchet-style center and mean radial distance
models.purpose: Summarize incident geography by a road-metric center and radius for residence profiling and buffer-zone scaling.
models.summary: After showing that a direct radial least-squares circle fit is unstable, the paper generalizes the Euclidean squared-distance centroid to road distance and defines radius as mean road distance from the minimizing center.

variables.definition: Candidate center of the incident pattern.
Location of incident i.
Literal x_n printed in the Euclidean centroid summand on page 8; context indicates x_i was intended.
Crime location variable used in the naive circle objective as printed.
Circle of radius r around x in the naive formulation.
Road distance supplied by MU-B-7273-ROAD-METRIC.
Average road distance from the chosen center to incidents.
Number of incident locations.

governing_equations.purpose: State the rejected naive radial circle-fit objective as printed.
State the Euclidean centroid objective exactly as printed before metric generalization.
Define the road-metric center as the minimizer of total squared road distance.
Define radius as mean road distance from the minimizing center.

equation_status.reason: The naive objective, Euclidean reference objective, road-center objective, and radius equation are displayed on pages 7-8.

objectives: Reject an unstable radial fit and compute a more stable metric-space center plus a representative radius.
constraints: The center is selected from the map domain.
The road distance is used in both center and radius.
The radius is the mean distance after center minimization, not jointly optimized radial residuals.

details: The admissible center domain and map boundary treatment are not stated.

parameter_estimation.method: Enumerate or search map points for the squared-distance minimum, then compute the arithmetic mean of incident distances.

steps: Evaluate the total squared road distance for candidate centers.
Choose a minimizing center.
Average incident distances to obtain r.
Inspect the induced road circle.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: No search resolution, tie rule, uncertainty interval, or perturbation criterion is stated for the revised estimator.

assumptions: Offenders avoid crimes very near home.
Travel effort across incidents is roughly comparable.
One center and radius adequately summarize the pattern.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: A finite grid makes the minimization computationally feasible, and Figure 1 exposes instability in the rejected objective; uniqueness, outlier sensitivity, multimodality, and sampling uncertainty of the replacement are not demonstrated.

models.computational_cost: The minimization appears to scan a finite map grid using precomputed distances; no grid size, complexity, or runtime is reported.
strengths: Generalizes a familiar centroid property to the domain metric.
Produces an interpretable center and scale for the residence branch.
limitations: Mean radius is not a jointly optimized best-fit circle.
A single center can obscure multimodal patterns.
The Euclidean reference formula contains a visible index typo.
missing_details: Comparison against spatial median or multimodal alternatives

models.family: buffer-zone geographic profiling score adapted to road distance
models.purpose: Rank grid cells as possible offender residences by balancing travel effort against near-home offense avoidance.
models.summary: The paper reproduces Rossmo's grid score and buffer indicator, sets f=g=1.2 from prior Manhattan-metric work, replaces norm distance with road distance, normalizes by K, and chooses B as half the road-center mean radius.

Location of offense i.
Number of offenses included.

Indicator equal to one inside distance B and zero otherwise.
Radius of the offender's assumed home buffer zone.
Rossmo distance-decay exponent, set to 1.2.
Rossmo buffer-term exponent, set to 1.2.
Road distance supplied by MU-B-7273-ROAD-METRIC.
Mean radius supplied by MU-B-7273-ROAD-CENTER-RADIUS.

governing_equations.purpose: State the original Euclidean/Manhattan-distance Rossmo buffer-zone score reproduced by the paper.
Select the inside-buffer versus outside-buffer term.
Record the exponents transferred from Rossmo's prior criminal cases.
Define the paper's road-distance Rossmo score.

governing_equations.source_expression: B=r/2 (stated in prose as half of the best-fit-circle radius)
governing_equations.purpose: Set the buffer radius from the preceding road-center model.

equation_status.reason: The original and adapted Rossmo scores, binary indicator, exponent values, and prose-defined half-radius rule are retained from page 9.

objectives: Rank candidate residence cells under a buffer-zone hypothesis and normalize the score field.
constraints: The binary indicator switches at road distance B.
f and g are fixed at 1.2.
B equals half the mean road radius.

details: The score is static for a supplied offense set.
Grid extent, singular-cell handling, and boundary normalization are not reported.

parameter_estimation.method: f and g are borrowed from Rossmo's Manhattan-metric optimization; B is heuristically set to r/2 without re-estimation under road distance.

steps: Compute road-center mean radius r.
Set B=r/2.
Evaluate the road-distance Rossmo contribution from every incident at each grid cell.
Normalize scores with K.
Plot colored fields and surfaces.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: No grid convergence, singularity treatment, parameter retuning, or normalization tolerance is reported.

assumptions: Offenders avoid crimes inside a home buffer.
Prior Rossmo exponents transfer to road distance.
One offender and one residence generate the series.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: No target-specific calibration identifies f, g, or the half-radius rule under the road metric; known residences are overlaid mainly on in-sample fields, and singular distances require an unstated numerical convention.

models.computational_cost: The score sums N incident contributions at every grid cell using precomputed road distances; no runtime or grid-size measurement is reported.
strengths: Uses the same road representation as the next-crime branch.
Provides inspectable maps and surfaces for two cases.
limitations: Exponents are transferred without road-metric retuning.
The formula has singular denominators at zero and at 2B unless regularized.
Known residences are not evaluated under a predeclared search-cost metric.
